$comment: The claims ladder of proofs/README.md, declared as DATA so a registry can read it
rather than parse prose. Hand-authored and never generated: the point of the manifest is
that a human decided which rung each claim sits on, and a generator would only be able to
restate what the code already says.
`level` is a CLOSED set — proved | tested | assumed | policy — and the four map onto the
README's four rungs: proved, differentially tested, assumed-and-stated, and not-claimed.
A `policy` entry is an exclusion carrying its reason, because an unstated exclusion reads,
to whoever finds it later, as a claim that failed.
A `proved` entry names ONE theorem, its model and the prover pin, so an evidence check can
resolve the theorem in the named model and the pin in the named file; lemmas the claim also rests
on are its `supporting` list, checked the same way. The field names follow the shared
claims-ladder schema; the `$provers` block below is commentary on what each pin means and is not
read. Nothing here is checkable by
reading this file alone, and that is the intended shape: the manifest says where to look,
the proof leg (proofs/check.ps1) is what looks.
Every later proof phase in this repository appends its claims here rather than starting a
second manifest.

fsharp-typed.what-it-proves: a construction the compiler refuses cannot happen at runtime. A claim on this prover names the type whose representation carries the invariant, the one mint, and the test cases that pin the visibility so a later public constructor cannot arrive silently. It is a weaker instrument than the F* prover - it says nothing about behaviour, only about who can build a value - and a claim resting on it says so

claims.claim: Given a parsed value, no combinator and no decoder built from them can diverge, throw, or reach a state that is neither an accept nor a named refusal. Quantified over ALL decoders, not one lemma per combinator, so it covers anything a consumer or a generator composes out of the algebra.
Which outcome, for which input, with the exact refusal - expected text, found text and path. The failure classification is exhaustive rather than merely non-empty.

The element accessor that both the positional-field and the index combinator are built from returns a value strictly smaller than its input, by the value model's own size measure. A decoder descending through it cannot recur forever, and not because of a depth counter.

evidence.note: carried in element_at's REFINED RETURN TYPE, so every descent consumes it at the call site. Since Phase 856 the accessor is INDEXED (item_at under a bounds test, element_of deciding presence) to match the array-backed Value.Arr, and the measure is stated over size rather than over the list spine the read no longer walks

claims.claim: The integer width rule is about INFORMATION, not signed range: a negative value never decodes into an unsigned target and fits a signed target exactly when it clears its minimum; a source no wider than its target always survives, sign reinterpretation included; a source wider than its target must fit its range; and the rule decides for every width class.

On a reader-producible value, an Int32 accept implies the payload carries no more than thirty-two bits of information - the union of the signed and unsigned 32-bit ranges. It deliberately does NOT imply the payload sits in Int32's signed range, because a negative decimal word arrives unsigned and the host's cast reinterprets it. That union is exactly the set on which the cast is a bijection.

evidence.premise: value_wf - the payload is within the width class its format byte declared. The one-pass reader produces only such values by construction; see the assumption `well-formedness-not-enforced-by-type`.

claims.claim: Over a reference API-record vocabulary - a nested record with a string, a bounded integer and a flag - the encoding of any value decodes, and decodes back to the value it started from. Not merely 'decodes to something': the decoder can never refuse traffic its own encoder produced.

The extracted model and the shipped algebra decode every covered wire-corpus case and every refuse-path mutation to the same outcome class, the same value, the same runtime type and the same refusal message. This is the only thing that says the proved model is about the code that runs.

evidence.family: Phase 787 - the proved model as oracle
cases: the extracted model agrees with production over every covered corpus case
the extracted model agrees with production over every refuse-path mutation
the model never throws, on any corpus payload, at any covered type
the reference vocabulary round-trips through the extracted encoder and decoder
evidence.runner: proofs/check.ps1 step 7, which asserts a CASE COUNT because a filter matching nothing reports success

claims.claim: The committed oracle is byte-identical to a fresh extraction from the checked module. Without this the committed file would be a claim; with it, a checked one.

A committed go-red case hands the model a bridge that has forgotten the source width class, and asserts the comparison catches it. It catches four cases and every one is the width rule losing. A differential never shown to fail agrees with whatever it is shown.

evidence.family: Phase 787 - the proved model as oracle
cases: the differential CATCHES a bridge that forgets the source width - the go-red case
and the width rule is what it catches

Since Phase 957 the extractor is Custard's F# backend (F* v2026.10.11, the release that made Custard the only extraction backend), run once over all nine models with --custard_split; until then the eight first-order models went through F*'s legacy F# printer, re-laid by a normaliser this repository wrote.

claims.mitigation: small enough to read in a minute; the byte-diff means a model change reaching for a tenth name fails the leg rather than compiling against a widened shim

claims.claim: Three payload facts come from the host rather than the model: a string's length, a binary payload's length, and a float's rendered text. Recomputing any of them would introduce a second implementation free to disagree with the host's - and for string length it demonstrably would, the two runtimes counting different units.

claims.mitigation: carried as data on the value model, so the model's refusals quote the host's own numbers

claims.mitigation: the lemmas that need it carry it as an explicit premise rather than assuming it away

claims.claim: Proof hints were removed from this prover, so the usual way to pin an SMT search is unavailable. The pinned release and its bundled solver, a margin on the resource limit, and three cold runs under --quake 3 are evidence of stability, not a guarantee of it.

claims.claim: The bytes-to-value pass is OUT of the theorem.
claims.reason: it is bounded - length against remaining on every length-prefixed read, and a depth ceiling - but bounded is not proved. This is the one place a binary-format proof framework would apply if it is ever wanted. A payload the reader itself refuses never reaches either decoder, and the differential skips it rather than pretending otherwise.

claims.claim: The System.Text.Json decode path is OUT.
claims.reason: its value carrier is undecided - the current JSON value model's numeric case cannot carry a 64-bit integer past 2^53, an exact decimal, or the source width

claims.claim: The reflection decode path is OUT, by construction rather than by omission.
claims.reason: it is an interpreter over an open, possibly recursive type graph walked with a mutable cursor, so 'total on every input' is not a well-formed statement about it - the input includes the type graph. That asymmetry is the whole argument for the closed value model. The path is reached through ONE seam on both hosts, `Codecs.resolveJson` / `resolveJsonEncoder` / `resolveMsgPack` (src/ToolUp.Platform.Core/Shared/Remoting/Codecs.fs), whose miss is the reflective path under `DecodePolicy.ReflectionFallback` and a refusal naming the type under `DecodePolicy.VerifiedOnly` (`Remoting.withDecodePolicy`): a deployment that composes the strict posture has no reflection decode or encode path left to be outside a claim.

claims.claim: One narrowing is unrefusable at the decoder.
claims.reason: the writer compacts a 64-bit value into bytes that ARE a well-formed 32-bit one - the shape a decimal's sign word travels in. The value model faithfully carries a 32-bit source and the information rule admits it, correctly, since refusing it would refuse every negative decimal the corpus pins. Closing it needs a writer that never compacts across a sign boundary, which is a wire break.

claims.claim: A trailing element past a record's declared fields is accepted, not refused.
claims.reason: a record decoder reads the positions it declares and ignores what follows, in agreement with the reflection reader. That is what keeps an additive wire change non-breaking, and it is the one evolution property this wire has.

claims.claim: A decoded value is well-typed. It is not authorised, not tenant-scoped and not semantically valid.
claims.reason: those are other boundaries' obligations; a decode theorem that implied them would be claiming something it cannot see

claims.claim: The date-only and time-only primitives have no combinator, so no model.
claims.reason: one of the two hosts' readers refuses both types outright, so a primitive for them would decode on one host and not the other. This ships a cross-host algebra or it ships nothing.

claims.claim: A record still decoding through the reflection path is outside every claim above.
claims.reason: the algebra is an opt-in replacement for a decoder that already works; the shipped default is unchanged. Which records those are is checkable: the boot line `RemotingDecoderFacet.describeCodecs` names every served record with a wire type `Codecs` does not resolve, and a `DecodePolicy.VerifiedOnly` mount refuses to start on one

claims.claim: For any ranking, any total verdict function and any policy assignment, no fact whose verdict is not-disclosable appears in the disclosed list.

The withheld count and the withheld projection are functions of the verdict list alone - the count is the number of not-disclosable verdicts and the projection is countBy-then-sortBy over their policy refs. The relational corollary states it over two rankings whose facts may differ in every field and even in TYPE: pointwise-equal verdicts give an identical projection, so no withheld fact's identity, rank or value was consulted.
Every disclosed (rank, fact) has fact at one-based position rank of the input ranking. A withheld member leaves a gap; a contiguous renumbering cannot satisfy this.

When anything was withheld, the gated summary's minimum, maximum and mean are absent; when nothing was, the summary is returned untouched; the existence-level fields ride through in both cases; and the gate fires exactly when some verdict denied. The biconditional is over the gate's ACTION - it does not say an absent magnitude implies a withheld member, since a summary over nothing comparable carries none to begin with.

Two rankings that agree on every disclosable fact and on every verdict yield IDENTICAL PopulationDisclosure records - the same disclosed list, the same withheld count, the same withheld projection - whatever the withheld facts' identities or values. No observation of the fold's output distinguishes one withheld population from another.

Which verdict, for which classification: Surfaceable is always disclosable, Internal never (naming the classification as its policy ref), and Restricted exactly when the resolver answers Some true - Some false and None both deny, so an unknown policy ref can never fail open. The conservative default denies every Restricted fact at every surface.

A release whose computed label carries a contributor is outside the trace lemma by construction: that release is a declassification, the contributor's data did influence it, and that is what a declassification means. What a determined reader could reconstruct across a SEQUENCE of such releases is a budget question, and a budget is a metered allowance, never a proof.

evidence.assumption: what a reader infers by combining declassified releases is bounded by the declassifications themselves

claims.mitigation: the boundary is explicit rather than implicit - q_free_of is taken before each release's own declassification, so the lemma's premise names exactly the releases it does not cover

claims.claim: The storage scope is assumed resolved. The theorem is about the computation's information flow; where the inputs and outputs are held, and under whose control, is a separate obligation it takes as discharged.

evidence.assumption: the storage scope that holds a computation's inputs and outputs is resolved and enforced

claims.claim: The derivation is modelled as a TREE. Production walks a graph with a memo table and a cycle guard. A memo cannot change a value; the content-addressed store is acyclic, and a tree is the acyclic case unfolded - where a graph shares an upstream the unfolding visits it twice and joins the same refs into the same label, which is immaterial under set equality.

evidence.assumption: unfolding production's memoised acyclic derivation graph into a tree changes no computed label

claims.mitigation: the differential checks the unfolding against the real walk on every fixture rather than leaving it asserted, and the host mirrors the cycle guard so a malformed graph cannot diverge there either

claims.claim: The theorem is about the LABEL, not the ordered ref list. Production keeps the inherited refs in nearest-declared-first order so the single deny ref it reports is unchanged from Phase 562. Order is a presentation fact about a refusal message; the label is the set, and the set is what is reasoned about.

evidence.assumption: the order production keeps inherited refs in is presentation only; the label is the set

claims.mitigation: the differential compares against production's own InheritedLabel, which is the set, so the comparison and the theorem are about the same value

claims.claim: The bridges in the differential host are hand-written. A label crosses as its own contents and returns through the shipped constructor; a transform crosses as its case; a fact's derivation is unfolded from the graph, mirroring production's private source-policy test rather than reaching for it. A defect in any of them would make the comparison compare the wrong thing.

evidence.assumption: the differential host's label, transform and derivation bridges map each value to the model value it denotes

claims.mitigation: short and case-for-case on purpose, and the committed go-red oracle beside them exercises the one field most likely to be got wrong; a bridge that mapped a join to a fold was shown to fail three arms before this landed

claims.claim: The inferred-lineage fallback is OUT of the theorem.
claims.reason: where no transform tree has labelled a fact, the walk falls back to lineage inferred from evidence linkage, and that inference is sound only where a derivation was routed through a series output - a derivation that was not is invisible to it, and an invisible upstream carries no taint at all. The theorem covers the COMPUTED side. The shipped code raises a finding naming every fact it fell back on, precisely so a verdict resting on inference cannot pass for one resting on computation, and this exclusion exists so the ladder does not quietly promote it.

claims.claim: A hostile operator is OUT.
claims.reason: root access, memory dumps, a modified binary and a compromised host are outside every sentence in the proved rung, and no amount of information-flow proof reaches them. Closing that gap is a hardware-attestation question, not a theorem. Stated rather than omitted because an unstated exclusion reads, to whoever finds it later, as a claim that failed.

claims.claim: That every pipeline declares its sources honestly is OUT.
claims.reason: a source nobody declared labels as clean. That is a POSITIVE statement the composition makes - which contributor a source belongs to is knowledge the composition has and the frame does not - and nothing here can detect a declaration that was simply wrong.

claims.claim: That the transform algebra stays closed is OUT.
claims.reason: the shipped contribution function is an exhaustive match, so a sixth transform case fails to compile until someone says what it reads. That is production's guard, not this theorem's, and the model would have to gain the case too.

claims.claim: A tuple combinator (Phase 800) accepts a positional array of exactly its arity and refuses every other value naming both arities - never a slice - and on an array of the wrong width the refusal is the arity check's refusal verbatim, so an element decoder is never reached. The element path is `[n]`, because a tuple element has no name to carry.

The several-field union-case form (Phase 800) hands the inner array to its field pipeline exactly when the array has the case's arity, and refuses a wrong-width array, a bare payload and a missing payload slot each by name with an empty path. The arity is at least 2 as a refinement on the model, because the writer emits a one-field case directly with no inner array.

Over the reference vocabulary widened by a leg - a pair and a union with a several-field case - the encoding of any value decodes, and decodes back to the value it started from, for every string-length function the host might supply. The union is also proved on its own so a failure localises to the several-field case rather than to the pair beside it.

The extracted model and the shipped algebra agree, outcome class, value, runtime type and message at once, over the corpus's tuple fixtures through tuple2 / tuple3, over Outcome paired both through payload and through fields, and over hand-built refusal shapes for both new combinators - including the one pinned contrast, an inner array with a trailing element that payload accepts and fields refuses. The widened vocabulary's round trip runs through the extraction, one instance per union case.

evidence.family: Phase 787 - the proved model as oracle
cases: the extracted model agrees with production over every Phase 800 refusal shape
the widened reference vocabulary round-trips through the extracted encoder and decoder
evidence.runner: proofs/check.ps1 step 7, which reads this family's case names from this registry and fails by name on one that stops running

claims.claim: DECIDED 2026-10-29 (Phase 957): the eight first-order models MOVE to Custard's F# backend on F* v2026.10.11, and the legacy F# printer and the layout normaliser retire. The decision was made for the phase by the release: upstream FStarLang/FStar#4653 (merged 2026-10-10) made Custard the only extraction backend, so v2026.10.11 - the first release carrying the two fixes Phase 955 reported - has no legacy printer, no --extract and no --custard_backend, and --codegen FSharp names Custard's F# backend. The measurement that was to decide on green is green: in one whole-program run split per module every model emits every definition under a module root (72 / 14 / 9 / 28 / 36 / 15 / 12 / 26 / 13 top-level bindings), every generated project builds on .NET 10 as generated (ModelInput's FS0058 is gone, #4626; RemotingDecode's seven refusals are gone, #4627), all nine modules transpile under Fable and the three the Fable pack runs do so in it, and every differential host is green on both hosts with its case counts unchanged. One model respelling, no theorem moved (RemotingDecode.item_at over List.Tot.hd / tl, because the match F* left incomplete by erasing a refinement is the model's to complete under the oracle's incomplete-match rule). UNTIL THEN (Phase 955, 2026-09-30, on v2026.09.27): the eight stayed on the legacy printer and the normaliser, only the array ring went through Custard.
claims.reason: What Phase 955 named as the trigger - a release in which every model's Custard project builds as generated - arrived with v2026.10.11, and with it the route Phase 955 stayed on was removed, so staying was not an option the pinned prover offered. What the move cost: every host bridge rewritten for Custard's spellings (one-constructor inductives as records, one-field records collapsed, unit thunks eta-expanded, module-qualified names kept by --custard_split), Prims.int as bigint on the Fable host, and one model respelling. What it bought: 759 lines of this repository's own layout parser and two hand-written Prims shims leave the trusted base; the support library the Fable host compiles against is derived from the generated one rather than written; and the eight models and the array ring are on one route, one extractor and one run. Phase 955's measurement and reasons are kept in proofs/README.md as the record of why the move waited one release.
